coherence.reasons: Both documents share the same governing thought (do not launch; back software) and the same five-part argument: market, unit economics, funding, alternative, decisions. X's executive-summary claims reappear as its section titles, and each slide carries one message. Y puts the six-condition hypothesis test up front, which is a good framing device, and its executive summary carries more of the key numbers (the best-observed loss of $1.76, the $18M network loss). However, Y's slide 7 breaks its own hierarchy: the title and text say the plan turns negative if AOV or rider productivity falls to the median, but its chart shows riders at +$0.22 and density at −$0.31. X's equivalent slide is consistent between title, chart and text. Y's slide 8 also says the store loses $6.17 'even if density reached the median', which does not match the page it cites (all drivers at the median). The difference is small because the storylines are otherwise the same.

judgment.reasons: The recommendations are substantively identical. Both decline the launch, back software-first with hires phased against signed contracts, build a store-based fast-delivery product for pipeline grocers, and set four re-entry triggers with a 90-day checkpoint. Both weigh the same three options (the full launch, a single pilot store, software-first) against the same criteria. Both reject the one-store pilot for the right reason: even the best observed density loses money, and the runway rule is breached in month 10. Both state the main risk to their own recommendation, a 34% ARR growth floor. Both land on the answer key's preferred recommendation and meet all its defensibility criteria. Neither proposes the capped, capital-light partner test, but the re-entry triggers drawn from customer-site data serve a similar purpose in both. There is no meaningful difference in the trade-offs weighed.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the required calculations correctly: −$6.17 at the median, −$1.76 with best AOV and best density combined, −$12.57 for the pop-up, a 41.5% CAGR, and $2.5M (about 6 months) left against the 12-month rule. Both give break-even AOVs of $63 and $50. Both apply the Zipcart fee, promotion cut and volume loss to reach −$1.05 at the median and a break-even of about 1,042 orders a day, and both compute customer payback. Neither states the roughly +$2.25 result at best observed density with the fee, though the break-even density implies it. The difference is accuracy. My recomputation of the one-driver sensitivity gives AOV −$0.73, riders −$0.31, density +$0.27 and promotions +$0.22. X's chart matches this. Y's chart assigns +$0.22 to riders, −$0.31 to density and +$0.27 to promotions, so the values are mislabelled and contradict Y's own stated conclusion on that slide. Y also claims the pop-up store would lose $6.17 'even if density reached the median', which is wrong: that figure needs all four drivers at the median, and density alone would leave a larger loss. X states this correctly ('even with every driver at the median'). X has no comparable errors.

revision.reasons: Both state the founders' hypothesis explicitly, break it into the same six necessary conditions, find none met and reverse it. Both grant what is true in the founders' view: the 40%+ market growth is real, and the pop-up was an early test. Both engage the Zipcart evidence that partly supports the founders, concluding that a profitable route may exist only at high density with a fee and is not shown in Parcelbird's data. Both turn that into concrete re-entry triggers rather than a flat rejection. Y places the hypothesis test at the front and X near the end, which is a presentation difference and not a difference in how the hypothesis is handled.

overall.reasons: The two documents contain essentially the same analysis, recommendation, alternatives, risk treatment and decision requests, and both match the answer key's preferred conclusion with all critical calculations right. Y is more compact and leads with the hypothesis test, which some boards would find more direct. But Y has a mislabelled sensitivity chart that contradicts its own slide title: it shows rider shortfall as still profitable and density shortfall as loss-making, the reverse of the truth and of its text. Y also has a smaller misstatement about density alone producing the −$6.17 loss. A founder on the board could use the chart inconsistency to challenge the analysis. X presents the same reasoning without these errors, so it serves the decision maker slightly better.
